passage: The pressure cooker let out its first whistle just as Kamal, twenty months, was stacking cups on the kitchen floor of the Kolkata flat. He jerked, his arms flew up, and he froze with his mouth open. Then came the wail. His mother Sharmila turned off the flame, knelt, and pulled him in. "Cooker," she said, pointing. "Loud. It's the cooker." At dinner, when it whistled again, he flinched, then pointed at the stove himself.

qa.q: What was Kamal doing when the cooker whistled?
qa.a: He was stacking cups on the kitchen floor.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling when his arms flew up and he froze?
qa.a: He was frightened by the sudden loud sound before he understood where it came from.

qa.q: Which choice by Sharmila helped, and why?
qa.a: Holding him and naming the source helped, because it turned a scary noise into something he could point at and understand.

qa.q: What is it like for Sharmila when Kamal wails at the whistle?
qa.a: She probably feels a pang of worry, but she stays calm so he can borrow her calm.

grounding: Shows a toddler's startle and fear at a sudden loud sound, and a parent helping him make sense of it.

passage:
"Just a small trim, beta," said Kishore the barber, lifting the buzzing clipper.
Zubin shrieked and flung his arms round his father's neck.
"Arre, it's only a noise," Kishore said.
"He's never heard it before," Papa said. "Zubin, look. Papa's hand." He held his own palm near the clipper.
Zubin peeked, then buried his face again.
"Shall we use scissors today?" Kishore asked, switching off the machine.
"Snip," Papa whispered. "Hear? Snip, snip."
Zubin turned his head a little and watched.

qa.q: What did Kishore offer to use after switching off the machine?
qa.a: Scissors.

qa.q: Why did Zubin fling his arms round his father's neck?
qa.a: The buzzing clipper was a new, scary sound, so he felt frightened and held on to the person who makes him feel safe.

qa.q: What worked in calming Zubin, and why?
qa.a: Switching to quieter scissors and letting him watch from his father's lap, because it removed the scary noise without forcing him.

qa.q: How might Kishore see a toddler screaming in his chair?
qa.a: At first he treats it as "only a noise", then he adjusts because he sees the fear is real.

grounding: Shows a toddler's fearful reaction to an unfamiliar buzzing sound at the barber's, and adults adjusting to it.

passage:
Creche note, Vidya, Ganesh Chaturthi week
A procession with dhol drums passed our gate at eleven. Jaya (2) dropped her crayon, ran to me and pressed her face into my sari, hands over her ears. She shook each time the drums came closer. I carried her to the back room, where it was quieter, and we watched from the window. By the end she took one hand off her ear to wave. I've told her mother the drums may bother her this week.

qa.q: When did the procession pass the gate?
qa.a: At eleven.

qa.q: What does Jaya pressing her face into Vidya's sari suggest?
qa.a: She was scared by the sudden loud drums and wanted to feel safe with a trusted adult.

qa.q: How could Jaya's mother use Vidya's note this week?
qa.a: She could keep Jaya a little away from processions and let her watch from somewhere quieter, holding her close.

qa.q: What would change if Vidya had made Jaya stand at the gate to get used to it?
qa.a: Jaya would likely get more frightened and learn that her fear isn't taken seriously.

grounding: Shows a toddler's fear of loud festival drums and a carer moving her somewhere quieter.

passage: In the village near Margao, Sabina was feeding her niece Maria lunch on the balcao. Rice went down happily. Then came one piece of bitter gourd. Maria's face crumpled, her tongue pushed the piece out, and she shuddered all over, shaking her head so hard her curls bounced. "Too bitter?" Sabina laughed, wiping her chin. Maria clamped her lips shut and pushed the spoon away with both hands.

qa.q: What did Maria push out with her tongue?
qa.a: One piece of bitter gourd.

qa.q: What does Maria's shudder and shaking head suggest?
qa.a: She found the bitter taste disgusting and wanted nothing more of it.

qa.q: What could Sabina try next time she offers bitter gourd?
qa.a: Offer a tiny piece mixed with rice on another day, without forcing, so Maria can get used to the taste slowly.

qa.q: How does Sabina react to Maria's rejection?
qa.a: She laughs kindly and wipes her chin, taking it as a normal toddler reaction rather than being annoyed.

grounding: Shows a toddler rejecting a new bitter taste with her whole body.

passage: Bao carried his daughter Soo-ah down to the water at the beach in Melbourne. She loved the sand, until a strip of wet seaweed wrapped round her ankle. She stiffened, lifted her foot high, and screeched, "Eee! Off!", nose wrinkled, hands flapping. Bao peeled it away. Soo-ah refused to put that foot down again and pointed at the dry sand until he carried her back up the beach.

qa.q: What wrapped round Soo-ah's ankle?
qa.a: A strip of wet seaweed.

qa.q: What does Soo-ah's wrinkled nose and screech suggest she felt?
qa.a: She was disgusted by the slimy seaweed and wanted it off her at once.

qa.q: How could Bao help Soo-ah feel okay near the water another time?
qa.a: Let her look at or poke seaweed with a stick from the dry sand first, and never push her towards it.

qa.q: What is it like for Bao when his plan for the water ends so fast?
qa.a: He may feel a little disappointed, but he accepts her reaction and carries her back.

grounding: Shows a toddler recoiling from an unpleasant slimy touch.

passage: I'm Mahima, and this summer I've been in charge of mango time with my baby brother Naveen. He loves the taste, but the juice running down his arms is another story. Yesterday he took two bites, looked at his sticky fingers, and held them out stiff, as far from his body as he could, making a "blech" face. When I wiped them he went straight back to the mango. Maybe it's the stickiness, not the fruit.

qa.q: What does Naveen love about mangoes?
qa.a: He loves the taste.

qa.q: What does Naveen's "blech" face suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: He seemed disgusted by the sticky juice on his fingers, even though he enjoyed the mango itself.

qa.q: What could Mahima do to make mango time easier for Naveen?
qa.a: Cut the mango into small pieces or keep a cloth ready, so he can enjoy it without sticky hands.

qa.q: How does Mahima make sense of Naveen's reaction?
qa.a: Mahima guesses it is the stickiness, not the fruit, that bothers him, but can't be sure.

grounding: Shows a toddler rejecting an unpleasant sticky feeling while still enjoying the food, seen by an older sibling in summer.

passage: At the spring fair in Warsaw, Marek tied a green balloon to his son Chidi's wrist, but the knot slipped. The balloon rose over the stalls. Chidi reached up with both hands, then went quiet, lower lip shaking, and watched it grow small. When it vanished he sagged against Marek's leg and cried in long, soft sobs. Marek crouched, held him, and said, "Gone. You liked that balloon." Chidi nodded into his coat.

qa.q: What colour was the balloon?
qa.a: It was a green balloon.

qa.q: What was Chidi feeling as the balloon grew small?
qa.a: He was sad at losing something he loved, shown by his shaking lip and soft sobs. 😢

qa.q: Which choice by Marek helped, and why?
qa.a: Holding him and naming the loss helped, because it let Chidi feel his sadness without being hurried out of it.

qa.q: What might Marek be feeling about the slipped knot?
qa.a: Maybe a little guilty, since he tied it, and sorry for Chidi.

grounding: Shows a toddler's sadness at losing a loved balloon and a parent naming the loss.

passage: I'm Nirmala, from the first floor. Our night watchman's daughter, Kiran, is about eighteen months and usually waves at everyone. This week she has been different. She sits on her mother's lap at the gate with her fist in her mouth, cheeks red, and whimpers when anyone tries to play. Yesterday she pushed away the biscuit I offered and turned her face into her mother's shoulder. Her mother says new teeth are coming. I don't know; she just looked so unhappy.

qa.q: What did Kiran push away yesterday?
qa.a: The biscuit Nirmala offered.

qa.q: What might Kiran be feeling when she whimpers and turns away?
qa.a: She seems uncomfortable and sad, maybe from sore gums, and too upset to play.

qa.q: How could the adults around Kiran support her this week?
qa.a: Let her stay close to her mother, not push play or treats, and check with a doctor if the discomfort keeps going or worries them.

qa.q: How does Nirmala see the change in Kiran?
qa.a: Nirmala notices the usual waving has stopped and feels for her, but only guesses at the reason.

grounding: Shows a toddler's unhappiness and discomfort, noticed by a neighbour.

passage: Winter in Shimla. Monday: Irfan, two, lost his red woolly cap somewhere on the Mall Road. At home he stood by the door calling "Topi! Topi!" and sobbed until his mother Binita rocked him to sleep. Wednesday: he wore his old grey cap, pulled it off twice, and cried quietly into her shoulder. Saturday: a shopkeeper had kept the red cap. Irfan grabbed it, hugged it to his chest and wouldn't let Binita put it on him.

qa.q: Where did Irfan lose his red woolly cap?
qa.a: Somewhere on the Mall Road.

qa.q: What does Irfan hugging the red cap to his chest suggest?
qa.a: He was relieved and happy to have it back after days of missing it.

qa.q: What could Binita do while Irfan grieves the lost cap?
qa.a: Comfort him, say that he misses it, and let him cry without rushing to replace it.

qa.q: What would change if the shopkeeper hadn't kept the cap?
qa.a: Irfan might keep missing it for a while, and Binita would need to help him slowly accept the loss.

grounding: Shows a toddler's sadness over losing a favourite cap, changing across a winter week.

passage: Oskar's father Chidi turned the handle of the old music box slowly while Oskar, two, leaned in close. Pop! A cloth clown sprang up. Oskar jolted back, eyes huge, mouth a perfect O, and sat down hard on the rug of their Stockholm living room. For a second nobody moved. Then Chidi laughed, and Oskar laughed too, a big surprised laugh, and pushed the clown down. "Again!" he said, reaching for the handle himself.

qa.q: What sprang up out of the music box?
qa.a: A cloth clown.

qa.q: What does Oskar's mouth making "a perfect O" suggest?
qa.a: He was startled and surprised by the sudden pop.

qa.q: How did Chidi help Oskar turn the shock into fun?
qa.a: He laughed right away, showing it was safe, so Oskar could read the moment as a game.

qa.q: What would change if Chidi had looked worried after the pop?
qa.a: Oskar might have read the surprise as danger and cried instead of laughing.

grounding: Shows a toddler's surprise at a sudden pop and how a parent's reaction turns it into delight.

passage: I'm Asif, Irawati's cousin. Last night the power went off in the middle of her dinner. Irawati, not yet two, stopped with the spoon in her mouth and went completely still, eyes wide in the candlelight. When the inverter clicked and the fan started turning again, she jumped, looked up at it, and then clapped and shouted "Fan!" I think it surprised her twice. She kept pointing at the fan for ages.

qa.q: What was Irawati doing when the power went off?
qa.a: She was eating her dinner, with the spoon in her mouth.

qa.q: What might Irawati have felt when the fan suddenly started again?
qa.a: She seemed startled at first and then delighted, clapping and shouting "Fan!"

qa.q: How could the family help Irawati during the next power cut?
qa.a: Stay close and name what is happening, like "lights off, lights back", so the change feels less sudden.

qa.q: How does Asif interpret Irawati's reactions?
qa.a: Asif thinks the dark and then the fan surprised her twice, though it is only a guess from her face.

grounding: Shows a toddler reacting to sudden changes in light and sound during a power cut, seen by a cousin.

passage: Early winter. Sunday: Jasleen, the new neighbour, ducked behind her dupatta and popped out at Salma, fourteen months. Salma's eyes went wide and she started to cry. Tuesday: Jasleen hid again, slowly this time. Salma stared at the cloth, held her breath, and when Jasleen's face appeared she gasped, then smiled. The next Sunday: Salma pulled the dupatta over her own head and yanked it off, squealing at Jasleen's pretend shock.

qa.q: What did Jasleen hide behind?
qa.a: Her dupatta.

qa.q: Why did Salma cry the first time Jasleen popped out?
qa.a: The sudden face from a new neighbour startled her, and the surprise felt scary rather than fun.

qa.q: What did Jasleen change that helped, and why?
qa.a: She hid slowly the second time, which let Salma expect the surprise and enjoy it instead of being frightened.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel when Salma cried?
qa.a: Perhaps a bit awkward and sorry, since she meant it as play, which is why she tried more gently.

grounding: Shows a toddler's reaction to peekaboo changing from fright to delight over a week.

passage: I'm Jasleen, and I jog in the colony park most evenings. There's a little girl, Urmila, maybe two, who comes with her father. He sits on the same bench every day, and she wanders to the sandpit, then the slide, looking back at him every few minutes. When she tripped yesterday, she didn't even cry until she'd run all the way to him. He picked her up, blew on her knee, and she went straight back to the slide.

qa.q: Where does Urmila's father sit?
qa.a: On the same bench every day.

qa.q: What does Urmila's habit of looking back at her father suggest?
qa.a: She feels safe knowing he is there, so she can explore and still check in.

qa.q: What is Urmila's father doing that supports her trust?
qa.a: He is in the same spot every time and comforts her quickly, so she learns she can count on him.

qa.q: How does Jasleen read the moment when Urmila fell?
qa.a: Jasleen notices she held her tears until she reached her father, and guesses he is her safe place.

grounding: Shows a toddler exploring with confidence because her father is reliably there, seen by a park regular.

passage: Night one in the new flat: Dolma, twenty months, woke three times and screamed until her father Sumit came. Each time he picked her up and said, "Papa's here." Night four: she woke once, called "Papa?" softly, heard his voice from the next room, and lay back down. Night ten: she woke, turned over, hugged her cloth rabbit and went back to sleep on her own.

qa.q: What did Sumit say each time he picked Dolma up?
qa.a: He said, "Papa's here."

qa.q: What does Dolma lying back down after hearing Sumit's voice suggest?
qa.a: She felt reassured and secure, trusting he was near even without seeing him.

qa.q: Why did Sumit's steady response help Dolma settle?
qa.a: Coming every time taught her that her needs would be met, so she felt safe enough to need him less.

qa.q: What is it like for Sumit during those first nights?
qa.a: It is exhausting to get up three times, but seeing her settle by night ten would feel rewarding.

grounding: Shows a toddler's trust growing over several nights as her father answers her every time.

passage: On the third night of Navratri the society courtyard in Ahmedabad was packed with dancers. Swati, two, sat on her mother Tanuja's hip, watching the swirling skirts. When Tanuja set her down, Swati gripped her dupatta, then let go to clap along. Every few minutes she spun round to find her mother's face, and Tanuja always waved back. Near midnight, tired and sweaty, Swati lifted her arms, and Tanuja picked her up without a word.

qa.q: Which night of Navratri was it?
qa.a: The third night.

qa.q: What does Swati letting go of the dupatta to clap suggest?
qa.a: She felt secure enough, knowing her mother was close, to join in on her own.

qa.q: What small habit of Tanuja's helps Swati feel safe in a crowd?
qa.a: Waving back every time Swati looks for her, and picking her up the moment she asks.

qa.q: How might Tanuja experience the night?
qa.a: She gets to enjoy the dancing while staying alert to Swati, and feels glad her daughter explores a little.

grounding: Shows a toddler feeling secure enough to explore a festival crowd because her mother responds every time.

passage: When Bhavna came back from the fields at sunset, her son Hrithik, two, was sitting on his aunt's lap on the charpai in their village courtyard. He saw his mother at the gate, slid off, and ran to her with his arms out. He pressed his cheek against her dusty sari and patted her face with both hands. When his aunt called him back for his roti, he shook his head and held on tighter.

qa.q: Where was Hrithik sitting when Bhavna came back?
qa.a: On his aunt's lap on the charpai.

qa.q: What does Hrithik patting Bhavna's face suggest?
qa.a: He felt happy and loving at seeing his mother after the long day. 🤍

qa.q: How could Bhavna respond to Hrithik's affection after a tiring day?
qa.a: Hold him for a few minutes before anything else, even if she is tired.

qa.q: How might the aunt feel when Hrithik won't come back for his roti?
qa.a: She may feel a small pang of being left out, but also understand that he missed his mother.

grounding: Shows a toddler's warmth and clear preference for his mother over another relative.

passage: Layla's grandmother Ines had been in hospital in Seville for a week. When she walked through the front door, Layla, twenty months, dropped her spoon, climbed down from her chair, and ran full speed into Ines's knees. She hugged them, then held up her arms. On Ines's lap she stroked her grandmother's hair and kissed her hand, over and over, humming.

qa.q: How long had Ines been in hospital?
qa.a: A week.

qa.q: What was Layla feeling when she ran into Ines's knees?
qa.a: She was overjoyed and full of love at seeing her grandmother again after missing her.

qa.q: How could the family support Layla while Ines recovers?
qa.a: Let Layla sit gently with Ines and show her softer ways to hug, so she can stay close safely.

qa.q: If you were Ines, what would you want from this moment?
qa.a: To hold Layla and enjoy the welcome, knowing she was missed.

grounding: Shows a toddler's love and warmth for a grandmother who cares for her.

passage: I'm Hafsa, from the flat across the landing. In the Christmas holidays Abhinav's mother started night shifts, so his grandfather looks after him in the mornings. Abhinav, about two, is friendly with everyone, but when his mother comes up the stairs at eight he drops everything, shrieks "Mumma!" and throws himself at her. Yesterday he held her face in both hands and kissed her nose. I can't know what he feels, but he doesn't do that with anyone else.

qa.q: What time does Abhinav's mother come up the stairs?
qa.a: At eight.

qa.q: What does Abhinav holding his mother's face and kissing her nose suggest?
qa.a: He feels deep love and delight for her, a special warmth he doesn't show anyone else.

qa.q: How could Abhinav's grandfather support him during these mornings?
qa.a: Keep his routine steady and talk warmly about when Mumma will come home, so the wait feels safe.

qa.q: How does Hafsa read Abhinav's greeting?
qa.a: Hafsa sees it as a clear sign of his preference for his mother, while admitting it is only what shows on the outside.

grounding: Shows a toddler's strong affection for his mother, seen by a neighbour.

passage: Monday, the first day at the creche: Pema, two, clung to her father's neck and screamed when he left. Vidya, the carer, held her by the window until she cried herself quiet. Wednesday: Pema cried at the door but let Vidya take her hand, and asked "Papa come?" again and again. The next Monday: she waved at the gate, cried for a minute, then went to the sand tray with Vidya.

qa.q: Who held Pema by the window on Monday?
qa.a: Vidya, the carer.

qa.q: What does Pema asking "Papa come?" again and again suggest?
qa.a: She was anxious about being apart and needed to hear her father would come back.

qa.q: What could Vidya and Pema's father do to ease the goodbyes?
qa.a: Keep goodbyes short and the same each day, and have Vidya answer "Papa comes after lunch" every time.

qa.q: What is it like for Pema's father to leave her screaming?
qa.a: It is probably painful and guilt-filled, even if he knows the crying usually passes.

grounding: Shows a toddler's distress at separation easing over the first week at a creche.

passage: At half past eight every morning in their Bengaluru apartment, Uma watched her mother pick up the laptop bag, and her face began to crumple. Today she grabbed the bag strap with both hands and wailed, "No go! No go!" Dolma, the neighbour who minded her, knelt beside her. Her mother kissed her, said, "After nap, I come," and left. Uma sobbed at the closed door until Dolma lifted her to the window to wave.

qa.q: What did Uma grab with both hands?
qa.a: The bag strap.

qa.q: Why did Uma's face begin to crumple when her mother picked up the laptop bag?
qa.a: She knew the bag meant her mother was leaving and felt anxious and upset about being apart.

qa.q: Which part of this goodbye helps Uma, and what could be added?
qa.a: The clear promise "After nap, I come" helps; a short goodbye ritual done the same way every day could help more.

qa.q: What might Dolma be feeling while Uma sobs at the door?
qa.a: She may feel sorry for Uma and a little helpless, so she offers the window wave as comfort.

grounding: Shows a toddler's separation distress each morning when her mother leaves for work.

passage:
"Ojas, Mumma is going to the wedding for a little while," Gurpreet said, pinning her dupatta. "Nani will play with you."
"No! Mumma!" Ojas wrapped his arms round her leg.
"I'll come back after your milk and one story."
"Mumma stay!"
"Beta, come see the lights," said Nani. The December balcony blinked with fairy lights.
Ojas cried harder and buried his face in her lehenga.
Gurpreet crouched. "Milk, story, Mumma. Say it with me."
"Milk... story... Mumma," he whispered, still sniffing.

qa.q: What will Ojas have before Gurpreet comes back?
qa.a: His milk and one story.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he wrapped his arms round Gurpreet's leg?
qa.a: He felt scared and upset about his mother leaving him.

qa.q: What worked in Gurpreet's goodbye, and why?
qa.a: Giving him a simple sequence to repeat, "milk, story, Mumma", because it helped him predict her return.

qa.q: How might Nani feel as Ojas cries harder at her offer?
qa.a: She might feel a little hurt but patient, knowing he just wants his mother tonight.

grounding: Shows a toddler's separation distress on a winter wedding night and a mother giving him a way to predict her return.

passage: At the small library in Copenhagen, Freya, the librarian, was carrying a stack of picture books when the top three slid off. Javier, twenty months, was sitting on the rug with his mother. Nobody asked him. He got up, toddled over, picked up one book with both hands and held it up to Freya. Then he fetched the second, and the third, and went straight back to the rug.

qa.q: How many books slid off Freya's stack?
qa.a: The top three.

qa.q: What might Javier have wanted when he held the book up to Freya?
qa.a: He seemed to want to help her, and maybe felt proud doing it, since no one asked or rewarded him.

qa.q: How could Freya respond to encourage this kind of helping?
qa.a: A simple warm thank you, using his name, is enough; no treat is needed.

qa.q: What is it like for Freya to be helped by a toddler?
qa.a: It is probably a touching surprise that brightens her day. 😊

grounding: Shows a toddler helping an adult pick up dropped books without being asked.

passage: I'm Thomas, from the house next door. On Sunday I saw Seema's grandmother hanging washing on the terrace when she knocked the peg tin over. Seema, who's about two, was playing with a bucket nearby. She stopped, looked, then started picking up the pegs one by one and dropping them back in the tin. Her grandmother hadn't said a word. When the tin was full, Seema carried it over with both arms and went back to her bucket.

qa.q: What did Seema's grandmother knock over?
qa.a: The peg tin.

qa.q: What does Seema going back to her bucket afterwards suggest?
qa.a: She seemed to help simply because she wanted to, not for praise, and felt content to return to play.

qa.q: How could Seema's grandmother show she noticed the help?
qa.a: Thank her warmly by name, so Seema knows her help mattered.

qa.q: How does Thomas see what Seema did?
qa.a: Thomas notices she helped without being asked and was not after any reward.

grounding: Shows a toddler spontaneously picking up spilled pegs for her grandmother, seen by a neighbour.

passage: Onam week in Kochi. First morning: Manjula dropped a basket of marigold petals while making the pookalam, and Simran, two, just watched. Third day: when petals spilled again, Simran squatted and scooped handfuls back into the basket without a word. Thiruvonam day: Manjula's hands were full with the payasam pot, and her slipper came off at the door. Simran picked it up and set it by her mother's foot.

qa.q: What did Manjula drop on the first morning?
qa.a: A basket of marigold petals.

qa.q: What might Simran have felt when she set the slipper by her mother's foot?
qa.a: Probably proud and pleased to be useful, since she did it without being asked.

qa.q: How could Manjula support Simran's new helping?
qa.a: Notice and thank her, and give her small jobs like sorting petals so she can keep helping.

qa.q: What would change if Manjula had scolded Simran for touching the petals?
qa.a: Simran might stop offering help, feeling her efforts were unwelcome.

grounding: Shows a toddler starting to help her mother without being asked over a festival week.

passage: Before every meal in their village house, Manjula took her granddaughter Mahima to the brass lota by the back step. Today Mahima, two, wanted her roti now. She stamped, shouted "No wash!" and sat down in the dust. Manjula poured a little water over her own hands and sang the soap song. Mahima watched, then held out her fists, rubbed them together, and splashed so much that both of them laughed.

qa.q: Where does Manjula take Mahima before every meal?
qa.a: To the brass lota by the back step.

qa.q: Why did Mahima stamp and shout "No wash!"?
qa.a: She was hungry and impatient, and the washing felt like it was keeping her from her roti.

qa.q: What worked in getting Mahima to wash, and why?
qa.a: Manjula washing her own hands and singing turned it into a game Mahima wanted to copy.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel about this daily routine?
qa.a: Patient, and quietly pleased that the habit is sticking even with some stamping.

grounding: Shows a toddler resisting and then joining a handwashing routine before meals.

passage: In their flat in Nairobi, Wanjiru sang the tidy-up song and held open the toy basket. Her son Hiroshi, two and a half, threw one wooden car in, then lay flat on his back and kicked. "No tidy!" She sat down beside him and dropped a car in herself, making a crash sound. He sat up. She did it again. By the fourth car he was racing her, and when the rug was clear he pushed the basket to its corner himself.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi throw in first?
qa.a: One wooden car.

qa.q: What does Hiroshi lying on his back and kicking suggest?
qa.a: He was frustrated and unwilling to stop playing just to tidy up.

qa.q: Which choice by Wanjiru turned it around, and why?
qa.a: Joining in with crash sounds made tidying a game, so he wanted to take part.

qa.q: What would change if Wanjiru had tidied everything herself?
qa.a: The rug would be clear faster, but Hiroshi would miss the chance to build the habit.

grounding: Shows a toddler resisting and then taking part in tidying up toys.

passage: I'm Damini, Sudha's older sister. In the summer holidays it stays light till late, and bedtime has turned into a fight. Last night Sudha, who is two, ran round the bed shouting "Not sleepy!" while Amma held her pyjamas. Then Amma drew the curtains, switched on the small lamp and started the same story as always. Sudha stopped, climbed under the sheet and held out her foot for the pyjamas. I think she likes knowing what comes next.

qa.q: What did Sudha shout while running round the bed?
qa.a: She shouted "Not sleepy!"

qa.q: What might Sudha have been feeling when she ran round the bed?
qa.a: She was probably excited and restless, since it was still light and bedtime felt too early.

qa.q: What helped Sudha settle, and how could the family keep it up?
qa.a: The familiar steps of curtains, small lamp and the same story; keeping that order every night helps.

qa.q: How does Damini explain Sudha's change?
qa.a: She thinks Sudha likes knowing what comes next, so the routine calms her.

grounding: Shows a toddler resisting bedtime in summer and settling once a familiar routine begins.

passage: In the kitchen of their village house near the church, Joseph, two, reached for the steel tumbler on the stove. "Joseph, no. Hot," said his mother Bhavna, just once, firmly. His hand stopped in the air. He looked at her, pulled it back and said, "Hot." Then he toddled to his grandfather's chair, climbed up, and laid his head on the old man's arm while Appachan stroked his hair.

qa.q: What did Joseph reach for on the stove?
qa.a: The steel tumbler.

qa.q: What does Joseph pulling his hand back and saying "Hot" suggest?
qa.a: He trusted his mother's warning and felt it mattered, so he accepted it without a fight.

qa.q: How could Bhavna build on Joseph listening to her?
qa.a: Praise him for stopping and keep her warnings short and calm, saving a firm "no" for real dangers.

qa.q: What might the moment on the chair mean to Appachan?
qa.a: It probably feels warm and touching to have his grandson come to him for comfort.

grounding: Shows a toddler accepting his mother's warning and showing affection to his grandfather.

passage: At the kerb outside the bakery in Buenos Aires, Liam held out his hand. "Hand, Santiago. Cars." Santiago, two, wanted to run after a pigeon, and for a moment he pulled away. Liam didn't raise his voice; he just waited with his hand out. Santiago looked at the cars, then at his father, and put his small hand in Liam's. On the other side he let go, hugged Liam's leg, and ran to the pigeon.

qa.q: What did Santiago want to run after?
qa.a: A pigeon.

qa.q: What might Santiago have felt when he pulled away for a moment?
qa.a: He felt tempted and eager to chase the pigeon, before deciding to listen to his father.

qa.q: What did Liam's calm waiting achieve?
qa.a: It let Santiago choose to follow the rule himself, rather than turning it into a fight.

qa.q: What would change if Liam had shouted?
qa.a: Santiago might have cried or pulled harder, making the crossing less safe.

grounding: Shows a toddler accepting his father's guidance at a road and then showing him affection.

passage: I'm Alka, from the house opposite. On Janmashtami evening, Sarita's family had the whole building over. Sarita, not quite three, kept trying to grab the butter pot from the little shrine. Her father said, "Sarita, that's for later," and she let go at once, though her lip trembled. Later, when her great-grandmother arrived, Sarita ran to her, bent to touch her feet the way her cousins did, then climbed into her lap and stayed there.

qa.q: What did Sarita keep trying to grab?
qa.a: The butter pot from the little shrine.

qa.q: What does Sarita's trembling lip suggest when she let go?
qa.a: She was disappointed but still accepted her father's word, showing she respects him.

qa.q: How could Sarita's father acknowledge how hard letting go was?
qa.a: He could thank her and tell her when she will get some butter later, so waiting feels fair.

qa.q: What is it like for the great-grandmother when Sarita climbs into her lap?
qa.a: It is likely a joyful, tender moment of feeling loved by the youngest in the family.

grounding: Shows a toddler accepting her father's limit and showing affection and respect to an elder during a festival.
